title: The Per-Unit System
description: Choose power and voltage bases, convert impedances between bases, and turn a one-line diagram with transformers into a simple per-unit impedance diagram.

study.title: Why per unit?
study.body: A per-unit (pu) value is an actual value divided by a chosen **base** value with the same dimension. On a sensible base, bus voltages sit near 1.0 pu, machine and transformer impedances fall into narrow, familiar ranges, and ideal transformers drop out of the circuit. Mistakes stand out too: a bus voltage of 1.7 pu is obviously wrong.

study.title: Choosing the bases
study.body: For a three-phase system choose a **three-phase power base** $S_{base}$ (one value for the whole system, often 100 MVA) and a **line-to-line voltage base** $V_{base}$ for each voltage zone (usually its nominal voltage). Current and impedance bases follow. With these bases, $S_{3\phi}$ and $S_{1\phi}$ have the same per-unit value, and so do line-to-line and line-to-neutral voltages: the factors 3 and √3 disappear from per-unit calculations.

study.title: Changing base
study.body: Nameplates give machine and transformer impedances in per unit on the equipment's **own rating**. Since $Z_{pu} = Z_\Omega\,S_{base}/V_{base}^2$, the same ohmic impedance on a new base is:

study.title: Transformers in per unit
study.body: Choose the voltage bases on the two sides of every transformer in the ratio of its **rated voltages**. Then its leakage impedance has the same per-unit value seen from either side, and the ideal transformer becomes 1 : 1, so it can be left out: in per unit a transformer is just a series impedance. Start in one zone and carry $V_{base}$ through each transformer with its voltage ratio. (The 30° shift of Y–Δ units is usually ignored in balanced studies.)

study.title: One-line diagram
study.body: A **one-line diagram** draws a balanced three-phase system as a single phase with standard symbols: generator G, transformers $T_1$ (13.8/138 kV) and $T_2$ (138/13.8 kV), a 138-kV line and a load. The transformers split the system into three voltage **zones**, each with its own $V_{base}$; buses are numbered 1–4.

study.title: Impedance diagram
study.body: Converted to per unit on 100 MVA, the same system becomes one series circuit: the generator's internal voltage behind its reactance, the transformers' leakage reactances and the line reactance, all in pu and with no transformers left. Shunt magnetizing branches are usually neglected.

study.title: Worked example: building the diagram
study.body:
$S_{base}$ = 100 MVA; zone bases 13.8 kV, 138 kV and 13.8 kV.
- G: 100 MVA, 13.8 kV, $X''$ = 0.20 pu: already on base, j0.20.
- $T_1$: 100 MVA, $X$ = 0.10 pu: j0.10.
- Line, j50 Ω: $Z_{base}$ = 138²/100 = 190.4 Ω, so j50/190.4 = j0.263 pu.
- $T_2$: 50 MVA, $X$ = 0.08 pu: 0.08 × 100/50 = j0.16.
- Current base in the generator zone: 100 MVA/(√3 × 13.8 kV) = 4.18 kA; in the line zone 418 A.

study.title: Sanity check: typical values
study.body:
On their own ratings:
- bus voltages: 0.95–1.05 pu in normal operation
- generator subtransient reactance $X''_d$: about 0.1–0.3 pu
- generator synchronous reactance $X_d$: about 1–2 pu
- transformer leakage reactance: about 0.05–0.15 pu, $X/R$ large
A result far outside these ranges usually means a wrong base.

steps.title: Per unit = actual / base
steps.body: Pick a three-phase power base $S_{base}$ for the whole system and a line-to-line voltage base $V_{base}$ for each voltage zone. The current and impedance bases follow from them:

steps.prompt: Find the impedance base for $S_{base}$ = {{Sb|VA}} and $V_{base}$ = {{Vb|V}}.
steps.explanation: $Z_{base} = V_{base}^2/S_{base}$ = ({{Vb|V}})²/{{Sb|VA}} = {{Vb^2/Sb|Ω}}. With kV and MVA it is simply kV²/MVA = {{(Vb/1e3)^2}}/{{Sb/1e6}}.

steps.prompt: Find the current base for $S_{base}$ = {{Sb|VA}} (three-phase) and $V_{base}$ = {{Vb|V}} (line-to-line).
steps.explanation: $I_{base} = S_{base}/(\sqrt3\,V_{base})$ = {{Sb|VA}}/(1.732 × {{Vb|V}}) = {{Sb/(sqrt(3)*Vb)|A}}. It is a line current: the rated current of a {{Sb|VA}} device at {{Vb|V}}.

steps.prompt: A {{Vb|V}} line has a series impedance of {{R}} + j{{X}} Ω per phase. Use $S_{base}$ = 100 MVA and $V_{base}$ = {{Vb|V}}.

ask.prompt: Find its reactance in per unit.
Find its resistance in per unit.

steps.title: Per-unit voltages
steps.body: With $V_{base}$ line-to-line and $V_{base}/\sqrt3$ as the line-to-neutral base, a bus voltage has the **same** per-unit value whichever you use. Normal operating voltages are 0.95–1.05 pu. Likewise $S_{3\phi}$ in pu equals $S_{1\phi}$ in pu, so per-unit three-phase work looks like single-phase circuit analysis.

steps.prompt: A bus in the {{Vb|V}} zone measures {{Vln|V|4}} line-to-neutral. What is its voltage in per unit?
steps.explanation: The line-to-neutral base is $V_{base}/\sqrt3$ = {{Vb/sqrt(3)|V}}, so $V$ = {{Vln|V|4}}/{{Vb/sqrt(3)|V}} = {{k}} pu, the same as $V_{LL}/V_{base}$ = {{sqrt(3)*Vln|V}}/{{Vb|V}}. Dividing a line-to-neutral value by the line-to-line base gives a value √3 too small.

steps.prompt: In per unit, the three-phase power and the per-phase power of a balanced system have the same value.
steps.explanation: $S_{3\phi,pu} = 3S_{1\phi}/S_{base,3\phi}$ and the per-phase base is $S_{base,3\phi}/3$, so $S_{1\phi,pu} = S_{1\phi}/(S_{base,3\phi}/3)$: the factor 3 cancels and both are equal.

steps.prompt: A fault study on a 100-MVA base gives a current of {{Ipu}} pu in the {{Vb|V}} zone. Find the current in amperes.
steps.explanation: $I_{base}$ = 100 MVA/(1.732 × {{Vb|V}}) = {{1e8/(sqrt(3)*Vb)|A}}. $I$ = {{Ipu}} × {{1e8/(sqrt(3)*Vb)|A}} = {{Ipu*1e8/(sqrt(3)*Vb)|A}}. Always use the current base of the zone where the current flows.

steps.prompt: Match each base quantity to how it is found (three-phase, line-to-line bases).
pairs: Chosen once for the whole system
Chosen per zone, set by transformer ratios
steps.explanation: Two bases are chosen ($S_{base}$ system-wide and $V_{base}$ in one zone, carried through the transformers); $I_{base}$, $Z_{base}$ and $Y_{base} = 1/Z_{base}$ follow.

steps.title: Changing base
steps.body: Equipment impedances are given on their own rating. The ohmic value is fixed, and $Z_{pu} = Z_\Omega S_{base}/V_{base}^2$, so on a new base:

steps.prompt: A generator rated {{Sr|VA}}, {{Vr|V}} has $X''_d$ = {{x}} pu on its own rating. Express $X''_d$ on a 100-MVA, 13.8-kV base.
A {{Sr|VA}} transformer has a leakage reactance of {{x}} pu on its own rating. What is it on a 100-MVA base (voltage bases equal to its rated voltages)?
steps.explanation: Only the power base changes: $X_{new} = X_{old}\,S_{new}/S_{old}$ = {{x}} × 100/{{Sr/1e6}} = {{x*1e8/Sr|pu}}. A larger power base gives a **larger** per-unit impedance, because $Z_{base} = V^2/S$ gets smaller.

steps.title: The transformer disappears
steps.body: Take the voltage bases on the two sides in the ratio of the rated voltages. Then the transformer's leakage impedance is the same in per unit from either side, and the ideal 1 : 1 transformer that remains can be left out. Example: a 100-MVA, 13.8/138-kV unit with $X$ = 19.04 Ω referred to the HV side has 0.1904 Ω referred to the LV side ($a^2$ = 100 times less). On 100 MVA: 19.04/190.4 = 0.1904/1.904 = 0.10 pu.

steps.prompt: A {{Sr|VA}}, {{VL|V}}/{{VH|V}} transformer has a leakage reactance of {{x}} pu on its own rating.

ask.prompt: Find the reactance in ohms, referred to the HV side.
ask.explanation: HV side: $Z_{base}$ = ({{VH|V}})²/{{Sr|VA}} = {{VH^2/Sr|Ω}}, so $X$ = {{x}} × {{VH^2/Sr|Ω}} = {{x*VH^2/Sr|Ω}}. From the LV side it would be {{x*VL^2/Sr|Ω}}: the ratio is $(V_H/V_L)^2$ = {{(VH/VL)^2}}, exactly the impedance-referral factor $a^2$.

ask.prompt: Find the reactance in ohms, referred to the LV side.
ask.explanation: LV side: $Z_{base}$ = ({{VL|V}})²/{{Sr|VA}} = {{VL^2/Sr|Ω}}, so $X$ = {{x}} × {{VL^2/Sr|Ω}} = {{x*VL^2/Sr|Ω}}. From the HV side it would be {{x*VH^2/Sr|Ω}}, $a^2$ = {{(VH/VL)^2}} times more, yet the same {{x}} pu.

steps.prompt: The line zone of a system uses $V_{base}$ = {{Vb|V}}. A generator feeds it through a {{VL|V}}/{{VH|V}} step-up transformer. Which voltage base must the generator zone use?
steps.explanation: Carry the base through the transformer with its rated voltage ratio: $V_{base,gen}$ = $V_{base,line}\,V_{LV}/V_{HV}$ = {{Vb|V}} × {{VL|V}}/{{VH|V}} = {{Vb*VL/VH|V|4}}. It differs from the generator zone's nominal {{VL|V}}, so impedances rated at {{VL|V}} must be converted with $(V_{old}/V_{new})^2$.

steps.prompt: If the voltage bases on both sides of a transformer are chosen in the ratio of its rated voltages, its per-unit leakage impedance is the same seen from either side.
steps.explanation: Referring an impedance across the transformer multiplies it by $a^2$, and the impedance bases on the two sides also differ by $(V_{base,HV}/V_{base,LV})^2 = a^2$. The two factors cancel, which is exactly why the transformer drops out of a per-unit diagram.

steps.prompt: A {{Sr|VA}}, {{Vr|V}} motor has $X''$ = {{x}} pu on its rating. Its zone has $V_{base}$ = {{Vb|V}} in a 100-MVA system. Find $X''$ on the system base.
steps.explanation: $X_{new}$ = {{x}} × ({{Vr/1e3}}/{{Vb/1e3}})² × (100/{{Sr/1e6}}) = {{x*(Vr/Vb)^2*1e8/Sr|pu}}. A small machine on a large base has a large per-unit impedance: it can supply little current compared with 100 MVA.

steps.prompt:
System (100-MVA base, {{VH|V}} base in the line zone):
- G: {{SG|VA}}, 13.8 kV, $X''$ = {{xg}} pu
- $T_1$: {{ST1|VA}}, 13.8/{{VH|V}}, $X$ = {{xt1}} pu
- line: $X$ = {{XL}} Ω
- $T_2$: {{ST2|VA}}, {{VH|V}}/{{VL|V}}, $X$ = {{xt2}} pu
Find the line reactance in per unit.
steps.explanation: In the line zone $Z_{base}$ = ({{VH|V}})²/100 MVA = {{VH^2/1e8|Ω}}. $X_{line}$ = {{XL}}/{{VH^2/1e8}} = {{Xl|pu}}.

steps.prompt:
System (100-MVA base, {{VH|V}} base in the line zone):
- G: {{SG|VA}}, 13.8 kV, $X''$ = {{xg}} pu
- $T_1$: {{ST1|VA}}, 13.8/{{VH|V}}, $X$ = {{xt1}} pu
- line: $X$ = {{XL}} Ω
- $T_2$: {{ST2|VA}}, {{VH|V}}/{{VL|V}}, $X$ = {{xt2}} pu
Find the reactance of $T_1$ on the system base.
steps.explanation: The zone voltage bases equal $T_1$'s ratings, so only the power base changes: $X_{T1}$ = {{xt1}} × 100/{{ST1/1e6}} = {{X1|pu}}.

steps.prompt:
System (100-MVA base, {{VH|V}} base in the line zone):
- G: {{SG|VA}}, 13.8 kV, $X''$ = {{xg}} pu
- $T_1$: {{ST1|VA}}, 13.8/{{VH|V}}, $X$ = {{xt1}} pu
- line: $X$ = {{XL}} Ω
- $T_2$: {{ST2|VA}}, {{VH|V}}/{{VL|V}}, $X$ = {{xt2}} pu
Find the total series reactance from the generator's internal voltage to bus 4, in per unit.
In the system of the diagram (100-MVA base; zones 13.8 kV, {{VH|V}}, 13.8 kV), the load at bus 4 absorbs {{PL|W}} at unity power factor and 1.0 pu voltage.

ask.prompt: Find the load current in per unit.
ask.explanation: With $V$ = 1.0 pu and pf = 1, $I = S/V$ = {{PL/1e8}}/1.0 = {{PL/1e8|pu}}. The same per-unit current flows through $T_2$, the line, $T_1$ and the generator.

ask.prompt: Find the actual current in the transmission line.
Find the actual current in the generator.
ask.explanation: $I$ = {{PL/1e8}} pu. Generator zone: $I_{base}$ = 100 MVA/(1.732 × 13.8 kV) = {{1e8/(sqrt(3)*13.8e3)|A}}, so $I$ = {{PL/(sqrt(3)*13.8e3)|A}}, {{VH/13.8e3}} times the line current, as the turns ratio requires.

steps.prompt: In a per-unit study the same current, say 0.6 pu, flows on both sides of a step-up transformer, while the currents in amperes differ. Why?
options: The current bases on the two sides differ by the voltage ratio, just like the actual currents
The leakage reactance cancels the turns ratio
$S_{base}$ is chosen differently on each side
steps.explanation: $I_{base} = S_{base}/(\sqrt3V_{base})$ with one $S_{base}$ and $V_{base}$ in the ratio of the windings. The actual currents scale inversely with voltage too, so the per-unit current is unchanged across the transformer.

steps.prompt: A load absorbs $S$ = {{P}} + j{{Q}} pu at a voltage of 1.0 pu. It is modelled as a series $R + jX$ impedance. Find $R$ in per unit.
To convert the {{VH|V}} line's reactance from ohms to per unit, you divide it by the impedance base of the 13.8-kV generator zone.
steps.explanation: Every element is converted with the base of **its own** zone: the line uses $Z_{base}$ = ({{VH|V}})²/100 MVA = {{VH^2/1e8|Ω}}. The 13.8-kV base is only 1.904 Ω; using it would make the line's per-unit reactance {{(VH/13.8e3)^2}} times too large.

steps.prompt: In the diagram (100-MVA base; zones 13.8 kV, {{VH|V}}, 13.8 kV): $T_1$ is {{ST1|VA}} with $X$ = {{x1}} pu, the line has $X$ = {{XL}} Ω, $T_2$ is {{ST2|VA}} with $X$ = {{x2}} pu (resistances neglected). The load at bus 4 absorbs {{P|W}} at pf {{pf}} lagging with $V_4$ = {{V4}} pu.

ask.prompt: Find the generator terminal voltage (bus 1) in per unit.
ask.explanation: Series reactance bus 1 → 4: {{X1}} + {{Xl}} + {{X2}} = {{X}} pu. $\mathbf S$ = {{p}} + j{{q}} pu, so with $\mathbf V_4$ = {{V4}}∠0°: $\mathbf I = \mathbf S^*/\mathbf V_4^*$ = ({{p}} − j{{q}})/{{V4}}. $\mathbf V_1 = \mathbf V_4 + jX\mathbf I$ = {{Vr}} + j{{Vi}}, $|\mathbf V_1|$ = {{sqrt(Vr^2+Vi^2)|pu}}.

ask.prompt: Find the generator terminal voltage in kV (line-to-line).
ask.explanation: $X$ = {{X1}} + {{Xl}} + {{X2}} = {{X}} pu. $\mathbf I$ = ({{p}} − j{{q}})/{{V4}} pu and $\mathbf V_1 = \mathbf V_4 + jX\mathbf I$ = {{Vr}} + j{{Vi}}, so $|\mathbf V_1|$ = {{sqrt(Vr^2+Vi^2)|pu}}. Times the 13.8-kV base: {{13.8e3*sqrt(Vr^2+Vi^2)|V}}.

ask.prompt: By how many degrees does $\mathbf V_1$ lead $\mathbf V_4$?
ask.explanation: $\mathbf V_1 = \mathbf V_4 + jX\mathbf I$ = {{Vr}} + j{{Vi}} pu with $X$ = {{X}} pu, so it leads by $\arctan$({{Vi}}/{{Vr}}) = {{deg(atan2(Vi, Vr))|°}}. Real power flows from the leading to the lagging bus.

steps.prompt: A generator in a 13.8-kV zone (100-MVA base) delivers {{S|VA}} at pf {{pf}} with a terminal voltage of {{V}} pu. Find its current in amperes.
steps.explanation: $|\mathbf S|$ = {{S/1e8}} pu, so $I = |\mathbf S|/V$ = {{S/1e8}}/{{V}} = {{S/1e8/V}} pu. $I_{base}$ = 100 MVA/(1.732 × 13.8 kV) = {{1e8/(sqrt(3)*13.8e3)|A}}, giving {{(S/1e8/V)*1e8/(sqrt(3)*13.8e3)|A}}. The power factor does not matter for the magnitude.

steps.prompt: A student converts a {{VH|V}} line's reactance to per unit with the impedance base of the 13.8-kV generator zone instead of the line zone. What happens to the result?
steps.explanation: $Z_{base} = V_{base}^2/S_{base}$: the 13.8-kV base is $({{VH/1e3}}/13.8)^2$ = {{(VH/13.8e3)^2}} times smaller than the line zone's, so dividing by it gives a per-unit value that many times too large.

steps.prompt: Put the steps of a per-unit study in order.
items: Carry $V_{base}$ through each transformer with its voltage ratio
Convert every impedance to the system base of its zone
Convert results back to kV, kA and MVA
steps.explanation: Bases first ($S_{base}$ once, $V_{base}$ zone by zone through the transformer ratios), then the impedances, then the circuit, and only at the end multiply by the bases of the zone where each quantity lives.

steps.prompt: A 13.8-kV generator ({{SG|VA}}, $X''$ = {{xg}} pu) feeds a 138-kV line through a {{ST|VA}}, 13.8/{{VHr|V}} transformer ($X$ = {{xt}} pu). The study uses 100 MVA and 138 kV in the line zone.

ask.prompt: Find the voltage base of the generator zone.
ask.explanation: Through the transformer ratio: $V_{base,G}$ = 138 kV × 13.8/{{VHr/1e3}} = {{Vbg|V|4}}, not 13.8 kV, because the transformer's HV rating differs from the line-zone base.

ask.prompt: Find the generator's $X''$ on the system base.
Find the transformer's reactance on the system base.
ask.explanation: On the HV side its rating is {{VHr|V}} against a 138-kV base: $X$ = {{xt}} × ({{VHr/1e3}}/138)² × 100/{{ST/1e6}} = {{xt*(VHr/138e3)^2*1e8/ST|pu}}. The LV side gives the same: (13.8/{{Vbg/1e3}})² = ({{VHr/1e3}}/138)².

steps.prompt: A current of 1.0 pu in a 13.8-kV zone is a larger current in amperes than a current of 1.0 pu in a 138-kV zone of the same system.
steps.explanation: $I_{base} = S_{base}/(\sqrt3V_{base})$: with 100 MVA it is 4.18 kA at 13.8 kV but only 418 A at 138 kV. The same per-unit current is ten times more amperes on the low-voltage side.
